title: Lithium Orotate and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Mix?
excerpt: Can you drink on lithium orotate? How alcohol's dehydration affects lithium in your kidneys, how the supplement differs from prescription lithium, hangover tips, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on lithium orotate? How alcohol's dehydration affects lithium levels, how it differs from prescription lithium, and warning signs to know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol and lithium orotate don't have a well-documented direct reaction, and the small amount of lithium in most orotate supplements is far below a prescription dose. But that doesn't make the combination risk-free. Lithium in any form leaves your body almost entirely through your kidneys, and the things that often come with a night of drinking, such as dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, and skipped meals, can make your kidneys hold on to more of it. Alcohol can also work against the very reasons people take lithium orotate in the first place, like steadier mood and better sleep.

**The quick rules:** Talk to your doctor before taking lithium orotate at all, and mention that you drink. If you do drink while taking it, keep it light, have it with food, drink water alongside, and stop well before you'd feel sick. On a morning when you are vomiting or can't keep fluids down, it's reasonable to skip your supplement dose until you are rehydrated. Be careful with ibuprofen and naproxen for a hangover, since they can raise lithium levels. Never take lithium orotate on top of prescription lithium unless your prescriber tells you to.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research about lithium, alcohol, and supplements. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and medications. **Talk to your doctor before using lithium orotate if** you have kidney disease, thyroid problems, heart rhythm problems, or a mood disorder; are pregnant or breastfeeding; take prescription lithium, diuretics (water pills), blood pressure medicines such as ACE inhibitors or ARBs, or regular NSAID pain relievers; or drink heavily on a regular basis. **Get medical help the same day if** you take lithium in any form and develop a worsening tremor, repeated vomiting or diarrhea, unusual drowsiness, confusion, slurred speech, or trouble walking. Call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) if you think you took too much. In an emergency, call 911.

> **Taking prescription lithium (lithium carbonate, Lithobid)?** This page is about the low-dose lithium orotate supplement sold over the counter. Prescription lithium is a different situation, with well-documented and serious alcohol risks, so read our [lithium and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol) instead and follow your prescriber's advice.

## What Lithium Orotate Actually Is

Lithium orotate is lithium bound to orotic acid, a compound your body makes on its own as part of producing building blocks for DNA. In the United States it is sold over the counter as a dietary supplement, usually marketed for mood support, calm, focus, or "brain health." People often call it "microdose lithium" or "low-dose lithium."

The key thing to understand is that the **lithium ion is the same** whether it comes from an orotate supplement or a prescription pill. Lithium carbonate (the prescription form used for bipolar disorder) and lithium orotate are just different carriers for the same element. What differs is the dose.

| | Lithium orotate supplement | Prescription lithium carbonate |
|---|---|---|
| Typical amount of elemental lithium | About 5 mg per serving (often labeled as 120 mg lithium orotate); some products contain 1 mg or less | Roughly 56 mg per 300 mg tablet, with daily doses often several tablets |
| How it's regulated | Dietary supplement. Not reviewed by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale | FDA-approved drug for bipolar disorder |
| Monitoring | Usually none | Regular blood tests for lithium level, kidney function, and thyroid |
| Approved uses | None | Bipolar disorder (mania and maintenance) |

So a standard 5 mg supplement serving contains roughly a tenth of the lithium in one prescription tablet, and a much smaller fraction of a full prescription day. That's the main reason the alcohol picture is different from prescription lithium, where the risks are well documented and serious. If you take prescription lithium, read our dedicated guide to [lithium and alcohol](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol) instead, because the stakes are much higher.

### What about claims that orotate "gets into the brain better"?

You'll see supplement sellers claim that lithium orotate crosses into the brain more efficiently than lithium carbonate, so a small dose acts like a big one. This idea traces back to promotion of the supplement in the 1970s. The human evidence for it is thin. Some animal research has suggested orotate may behave differently from carbonate in the body, and other older animal work raised questions about how it affects the kidneys. Neither question has been settled with good human studies. The safest assumption is simple: **lithium is lithium.** Treat the supplement with the same basic respect you'd give any product that contains it.

## How Alcohol and Lithium Interact: The Kidney Connection

Lithium isn't broken down by the liver the way most drugs are. Your kidneys filter it out of your blood and pass it in your urine. The catch is that your kidneys treat lithium a lot like sodium (salt). Whenever your body is low on fluid or salt, your kidneys try to hold on to sodium, and they hold on to lithium along with it. Less lithium leaves, and more stays in your blood.

Here is how a night of drinking can feed into that:

1. **Alcohol makes you pee more.** Alcohol blocks a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to save water. With less of it, you lose more fluid than you take in. Our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains this in more detail.
2. **Vomiting and diarrhea drain fluid and salt fast.** These are common after heavy drinking, and they are the classic triggers for lithium building up in people on prescription doses.
3. **Skipped meals and sweating add to it.** Not eating much the next day, dancing in a hot room, or a hot climate all reduce your fluid and salt intake or increase losses.
4. **Hangover painkillers can pile on.** NSAIDs like ibuprofen and naproxen reduce how much lithium your kidneys clear. They are one of the best-known causes of rising lithium levels in people on the prescription drug.

At prescription doses, this chain of events is a recognized route to lithium toxicity. At supplement doses, there's much more room before levels reach a dangerous range, so a single light night out is unlikely to cause trouble for a healthy person. But "unlikely" is not "impossible," and the risk grows when several of these factors stack up, when you take more than the label says, or when you also take medicines that affect the kidneys.

### What alcohol does on the mood side

The second interaction isn't chemical. People usually take lithium orotate hoping for steadier mood, less irritability, or better sleep. Alcohol tends to work against all three. It's a depressant, so it can lower mood the next day. It breaks up sleep in the second half of the night. And the day-after "hangxiety" many people feel is a real effect of the brain rebounding from alcohol's calming effect. If you're taking a supplement for mood and drinking regularly, the drinking may be undoing much of what you hoped the supplement would do.

If you take lithium orotate because of an actual mood disorder, such as depression or bipolar disorder, that's a conversation to have with a doctor rather than a supplement shelf. Alcohol can make mood disorders harder to manage, and a microdose supplement is not a treatment for them.

## Can You Drink on Lithium Orotate?

For a healthy adult taking a standard low-dose supplement as directed, an occasional drink or two with food is generally considered a low-risk situation. Your doctor is the right person to confirm that for you. Here's how to keep the risk as low as possible if you do drink:

- **Keep it light.** One or two drinks, spaced out, is a very different situation from a long night that ends with you feeling sick.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks helps offset the fluid alcohol makes you lose.
- **Eat a real meal.** Food slows alcohol absorption and gives you some salt, which helps your kidneys hold their normal balance.
- **Stop before you feel sick.** Vomiting is the point where fluid and salt losses really add up.
- **Don't double up the next day.** If you missed a dose, don't take two to "catch up."
- **Watch the heat.** Drinking in a hot place, at a festival, or after a workout adds sweating on top of alcohol's fluid loss.

### When to skip the supplement

It's reasonable to skip your lithium orotate dose, and check with your doctor, if:

- You are vomiting or have diarrhea and can't keep fluids down
- You are very dehydrated, dizzy when you stand, or barely urinating
- You've had a much heavier night than usual
- You've just started a new medication that affects the kidneys

Skipping a microdose supplement for a day is very unlikely to cause any harm. That is not true of prescription lithium, where you should never stop or change a dose without talking to your prescriber.

## Lithium Orotate and Hangovers

There's no good evidence that lithium orotate makes hangovers better, and no research looking at whether it makes them worse. What we can say is that the main features of a bad hangover, especially dehydration and any vomiting or diarrhea, are the same conditions that slow down lithium clearance. So the morning after is the part of the night to pay attention to.

A sensible hangover routine if you take lithium orotate:

1. **Rehydrate first.** Water, plus something with a bit of salt, such as an oral rehydration drink, broth, or a salty snack. You're replacing both fluid and sodium.
2. **Eat when you can.** Toast, crackers, rice, eggs, or soup are all easy options.
3. **Think twice about the painkiller.** Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), and high-dose aspirin are NSAIDs. In people on prescription lithium they are a known cause of rising lithium levels. Whether that matters at supplement doses isn't well studied, but there's no reason to stack an NSAID on top of dehydration if you can avoid it. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) doesn't affect lithium levels, but it has its own alcohol risks for the liver, so follow its label carefully and ask a pharmacist which option fits you.
4. **Skip the supplement if you can't keep fluids down.** Take it again once you're eating and drinking normally.
5. **Notice symptoms that don't fit a normal hangover.** A tremor that's getting worse instead of better, confusion, slurred speech, or unsteadiness after you've sobered up are reasons to get checked. More on that below.

The shakes after drinking are common and usually come from alcohol's rebound effects on your nervous system and blood sugar, not from lithium. Our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains the usual causes. But because a worsening tremor is also an early sign of too much lithium, a tremor that keeps getting worse over the day deserves attention if you take lithium in any form.

## Lithium Orotate Side Effects That Overlap With Drinking

One reason to be careful is that the side effects of lithium and the effects of alcohol look alike. At typical supplement doses, most people notice nothing. When side effects do show up, they can include:

- Nausea or an upset stomach
- Mild hand tremor
- Feeling tired or drowsy
- Increased thirst or urination
- Loose stools

Every one of those also shows up during a hangover. That overlap makes it easy to dismiss a real problem as "just a rough morning." If symptoms are stronger than your usual hangover, last longer than a day, or keep getting worse after the alcohol has cleared, don't assume it's the drinks.

### Signs of too much lithium

Lithium toxicity is rare at supplement doses, but it has been reported. A case report in the *Journal of Medical Toxicology* in 2007 described a young woman who swallowed a large number of lithium orotate tablets bought online and developed nausea, vomiting, and tremor. She recovered with hospital care. The point isn't that a normal dose is dangerous. It's that "it's just a supplement" doesn't mean you can't take too much.

**Get medical help if you take lithium in any form and notice:**

- Repeated vomiting or diarrhea
- A coarse or worsening tremor
- Unusual drowsiness or sluggishness
- Muscle weakness, twitching, or jerking
- Unsteadiness or trouble walking
- Slurred speech
- Confusion or not making sense

**Call 911 for** severe confusion, fainting, a seizure, or someone who is very hard to wake. For anything that might be an overdose, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US), even if the person seems fine. Bring the supplement bottle with you if you go to the hospital, so staff can see how much lithium it contains.

## Medications and Conditions That Raise the Stakes

The risk from drinking on lithium orotate goes up if anything else is already pushing your lithium level higher or your kidneys harder. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about the supplement if you take any of these:

| Medicine or condition | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Prescription lithium | Adds to your total lithium dose. Don't combine without your prescriber's approval. |
| Thiazide diuretics (water pills), such as hydrochlorothiazide | Known to raise lithium levels by changing how the kidneys handle sodium. |
| ACE inhibitors and ARBs (common blood pressure medicines), such as lisinopril or losartan | Can raise lithium levels. |
| NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen | Reduce lithium clearance. |
| Kidney disease | Lithium depends on the kidneys to leave the body. |
| Thyroid disease | Lithium can affect the thyroid at prescription doses. |
| Heart rhythm problems | Lithium can affect heart rhythm at higher levels. |
| Pregnancy or breastfeeding | Lithium crosses the placenta and into breast milk. |

These interactions are best documented with prescription lithium. Nobody can say exactly how much they matter at a 5 mg supplement dose, which is exactly why a pharmacist or doctor should look at your full list. For a broader view of how alcohol interacts with common medicines, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Does Lithium Orotate Work, and Is It Worth It If You Drink?

It's fair to ask whether the supplement is doing enough to be worth thinking about at all. The honest answer is that the evidence for microdose lithium orotate in people is limited.

The interest in low-dose lithium mostly comes from **observational studies** that compared natural lithium levels in drinking water across different regions with local rates of suicide and other outcomes. Several of these studies found that areas with more natural lithium in the water tended to have lower suicide rates. That's an interesting finding, but it shows a link, not cause and effect, and the amounts of lithium in water are tiny. There are no large, well-designed trials showing that a lithium orotate supplement improves mood, anxiety, or memory in healthy adults.

That doesn't mean it does nothing. It means you're taking a product with modest evidence behind it, and it makes sense to weigh it against things with clearer benefits. If you drink regularly and you're reaching for a supplement because you feel low, anxious, or wired the day after, cutting back on the drinking is likely to help your mood and sleep more than any supplement. Our guide to [ashwagandha and alcohol](/never-hungover/ashwagandha-and-alcohol) covers another popular calm-and-mood supplement and how it fits with drinking, and our [magnesium and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) covers a mineral heavy drinking tends to deplete.

## Lithium Orotate vs. Prescription Lithium With Alcohol: The Key Differences

Since people often mix up the two, here's the side-by-side on alcohol specifically:

- **Same mechanism, different scale.** Both carry the same risk pathway: dehydration and salt loss make the kidneys hold on to lithium. With a prescription dose, that can push a person into toxicity. With a supplement, there's far more margin.
- **Monitoring.** People on prescription lithium have blood levels checked, so their doctor knows where they stand. Supplement users usually have no idea what their level is, which is one more reason to keep drinking light.
- **Stopping and skipping.** Skipping a supplement dose for a day is generally harmless. Stopping prescription lithium suddenly can trigger a relapse of mania or depression and should only be done with your prescriber.
- **The condition being treated.** Prescription lithium treats bipolar disorder, a condition where alcohol can be especially disruptive. Supplement users are often generally healthy people chasing a mood edge.

If you take both, or you're thinking of switching from prescription lithium to a supplement, talk to your prescriber first. Lithium orotate is not a replacement for prescribed lithium, and the doses aren't comparable.

## Where DHM Fits In

Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that many people take before or after drinking. Most of its research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, and it has been studied mainly for how it may affect alcohol metabolism and the liver. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents dehydration, and it does nothing to change how your kidneys handle lithium. It isn't a reason to drink more while taking lithium orotate.

The combination of DHM and lithium orotate hasn't been studied, so check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding it. If they're comfortable with it and you want to try DHM, a simple single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). A single-ingredient product keeps things simple when you're already taking another supplement. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM alongside common medicines.

Whatever you take, the things that actually protect you with any form of lithium are the basic ones: drink less, drink water alongside, eat, and don't let a night out end in vomiting.

## The Bottom Line

- Lithium orotate contains the same lithium as prescription lithium, just in a much smaller amount, usually about 5 mg per serving.
- There's no well-documented direct reaction with alcohol. The risk comes from dehydration and salt loss, which make your kidneys hold on to lithium.
- An occasional light drink with food and water is generally low-risk for a healthy adult on a standard supplement dose. Confirm that with your doctor.
- Vomiting, diarrhea, heat, heavy drinking, NSAID painkillers, and certain blood pressure medicines all push lithium levels in the same direction.
- Skip the supplement on a day you can't keep fluids down, and never combine it with prescription lithium without your prescriber's approval.
- Know the signs of too much lithium. A worsening tremor, confusion, slurred speech, or unsteadiness after you've sobered up needs medical attention.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking lithium orotate?**

Many people take a low-dose lithium orotate supplement and have an occasional drink, and there is no well-documented direct chemical reaction between the two. The risk is indirect. Lithium leaves your body through your kidneys, and the dehydration and salt loss that come with heavy drinking, vomiting, or diarrhea can make your kidneys hold on to more lithium. Keep drinking light, have water and food alongside, don't drink to the point of being sick, and talk to your doctor first, especially if you take other medicines or have kidney, thyroid, or heart problems.

**Is lithium orotate the same as prescription lithium?**

No. Both deliver the same lithium ion, but the amount is very different. A typical lithium orotate supplement provides about 5 mg of elemental lithium per serving, while a single 300 mg tablet of prescription lithium carbonate provides roughly 56 mg. Prescription lithium is an FDA-approved drug for bipolar disorder, dosed and monitored with blood tests. Lithium orotate is sold as a dietary supplement, is not approved to treat any condition, and is not a substitute for prescription treatment.

**Can lithium orotate make a hangover worse?**

There is no good research on lithium orotate and hangovers specifically. What we do know is that a hangover often involves dehydration, and sometimes vomiting or diarrhea, which are exactly the conditions that make the kidneys clear lithium more slowly. At supplement doses this is unlikely to cause a problem for most healthy people, but it is a reason to rehydrate properly, skip ibuprofen and naproxen unless your doctor has cleared them, and consider skipping your supplement dose on a morning when you can't keep fluids down.

**How long after taking lithium orotate can I drink?**

There is no official waiting period, and spacing the two by a few hours doesn't change the main risk, which comes from dehydration and salt loss over the following day. What matters more is how much you drink, whether you stay hydrated, and whether you get sick. If you drink regularly or heavily, ask your doctor whether the supplement makes sense for you at all.

**What are the signs of lithium toxicity?**

Early signs include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, a worsening hand tremor, drowsiness, and feeling weak or unsteady. More serious signs include slurred speech, confusion, muscle twitching, trouble walking, and a very coarse tremor. Many of these look like being drunk or hungover, which is why they can be missed. If you take lithium in any form and have these symptoms, especially after vomiting or diarrhea, call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or seek medical care. For severe confusion, fainting, or a seizure, call 911.

**Can I take lithium orotate with prescription lithium?**

Not unless the doctor who prescribes your lithium specifically tells you to. Adding a supplement on top of prescription lithium raises your total lithium dose, and prescription lithium already has a narrow safe range that is checked with blood tests. Tell your prescriber about every supplement you take.

**Does lithium orotate interact with ibuprofen after drinking?**

Ibuprofen, naproxen, and other NSAIDs are well known to raise blood lithium levels in people on prescription lithium, because they reduce how much lithium the kidneys clear. Whether that matters at supplement doses hasn't been well studied, but combining an NSAID with dehydration from drinking stacks two things that push lithium in the same direction. Ask a pharmacist which pain reliever suits you before you need one.

**Is it safe to take DHM with lithium orotate?**

There is no good evidence either way, because the combination hasn't been studied. DHM is not known to affect how the kidneys handle lithium, but no supplement should be combined with lithium in any form without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first. DHM also does nothing to prevent the dehydration that is the real concern with alcohol and lithium.
